newsitem.title: USA: U.S. homebuilding levels off at healthy pace in July.
newsitem.headline: U.S. homebuilding levels off at healthy pace in July.

text.p: The building rate for new homes and apartments leveled off in July at a healthy pace, a report from the Commerce Department on Tuesday showed, as strong job growth leupport to the housing sector.

Builders broke ground on new homes at a seasonally adjusted annual rate of 1.447 million a year in July. That was unchanged from June when starts rose a downward revised 3.2 percent from May instead of increasing 4.8 percent as the government previously reported.
Analysts said it appeared the pace of building activity was moderating at mid-year, albeit at a strong level, following a boom at the start of the year that was spurred by exceptionally mild weather.

The July starts report, published just as Federal Reserve policymakers gathered to consider interest-rate strategy, was welcomed as another influence likely to persuade the Fed against raising rates to curb the economy's expansion.
"This clearly was additional support in what already was a strong case for no (Fed) action," said Paul Taylor, an economist for America's Community Bankers.

The only region where homebuilding put on steam in July was in the Northeast. Starts there surged 41.4 percent to a rate of 157,000 a year, the strongest monthly gain since a 41.9 percent increase in November 1994.
In the Midwest, building rates were down 3.7 percent to 289,000, in the South they fell 2.4 percent to 663,000 and in the West they fell 5.3 percent to 338,000 a year.

But analysts said there was no likelihood of a developing downturn in the housing sector, either on its sales or building sides. Mortgage rates remain favorable by historical standards while brisk rates of job creation and exuberant levels of consumer optimism were expected to put a floor under building activity.

"There is no real sign of weakness in the housing sector," said economist Richard Berner of Mellon Bank in Pittsburgh. Similarly, economist David Seiders from the National Association of Home Builders said lean inventories and a solid economy favored a steady pace of building activity ahead.

"It is a market that is pretty much settling around a plateau of around 1.44 (million new homes a year) or 1.45 and that's going to be a sustainable pace," Seiders said. That would be only 2 percent to 3 percent below last year's sturdy 1.48-million-unit building rate.
During July, starts on new single-family homes advanced 2.7 percent to 1.141 million a year, but apartment construction slumped 8.9 percent to a rate of 306,000.

New applications for building permits increased 1.4 percent in July to a seasonally adjusted annual rate of 1.422 million after falling 2.1 percent in June -- another indication that building activity likely will continue at a healthy level.
On Monday, the National Association of Home Builders said its index of market activity climbed in August to 58 from 56 in July.

"Declining interest rates during most of the month helped improve customer traffic, current sales and builder outlook, the three components of the housing market index," said Kent Colton, the association's executive vice president.
